justification: Formed a fresh read of the current build before opening any prior round's file. Against the target query ('array vs list c#', 'dynamic array'), the best-ranking existing results are pure syntax/API references with no memory model, no measurements and no diagrams; this article's traversal-order benchmark, byte-offset arithmetic verified with Unsafe.ByteOffset, four hand-drawn figures, and the Insert/RemoveAt shift diagram put it well ahead of them on depth and illustration, which is why the score sits above 'decent personal blog' territory. It is held below 8.5 by one persistent, verified-worse shell defect and a short tail of real but minor rendering nits, not by effort. Ran `node tools/verify-page.mjs --drafts /data-structures/arrays-and-dynamic-arrays/` three times as instructed: performance scored 87, 79, and 78 (accessibility/best-practices/SEO were 100 in all three). Median 79, best 87 — both still below the pass gate's 90, and this is not an improvement on round 3's single measurement of 87: two of three runs this round were markedly worse. The failing/borderline Lighthouse items on the last run were First Contentful Paint 3.0s, Largest Contentful Paint 3.1s, Total Blocking Time 400ms, Max Potential FID 310ms, main-thread work 2.1s, ~11 KiB unused CSS, blocked back/forward-cache restoration, ~255 KiB document-request latency, a failing forced-reflow insight and a failing network-dependency-tree insight — the same shape of failure as round 3, just landing lower this run. I cannot attribute this swing to article content changes (word count and code-block count grew only marginally, 5902→5954 words, 35→35 code blocks, 4 figures unchanged) rather than machine load, but three runs is what the brief calls for and the real numbers are what they are. Checked the two specific fixes named for this round directly against the current source and confirmed both are genuine, not cosmetic: (1) the 'offsets' program (id=offsets) no longer inlines three long Gap(...) calls into one WriteLine; it now assigns each to a short-named variable (g01, g10, g23) on its own line and the final WriteLine reduces to `$" [0,1] {g01} [1,0] {g10}" + $" [2,3] {g23}"` — verified fully visible with no fade-clip on mobile-dark part04 and mobile-light part04, where round 3 had flagged exactly this line clipping after 'ref gr'. (2) The tiled program's (id=tiled) closing Console.WriteLine, previously two long interpolated lines that clipped, is now four short lines (`$"n={n,4}  col/row"`, `$" {col / row,5:F1}"`, `$"  tiled/row"`, `$" {tiled / row,5:F1}"`) — verified fully visible with no clipping on mobile-dark part09 and mobile-light part09. Also spot-checked the indexer-terminology paragraph ('That indexer returns T by value, not by reference...' through the a[i]-is-not-an-indexer explanation) on mobile-dark part13: it is ordinary prose, wraps normally, nothing clips. One new, previously unflagged clipping instance turned up while re-reading every mobile-dark part fresh: in the same 'offsets' program, the `Show<T>` helper's own `Console.WriteLine($"{type,-20}{one,4}{three,5}");` line (used to print the int[]/long[]/Sample[]/string[] step sizes) was not touched by the round-3 fix and clips at 390px (mobile-dark part04) — low-impact since the output panel directly below shows the actual numbers, but the same class of bug the round-3 fix addressed one line above it. Read every desktop-light part (fold + 01-18) and every mobile-dark part (fold + 01-28); spot-checked desktop-dark (fold, parts 09, 16) and mobile-light (fold, parts 09, 19) for theme correctness — all four figures render with correct colors, dashed/solid states and legible labels in both themes at both widths, mobileOverflowPx is 0, consoleErrors and brokenLinks are both 0. Not fixed, carried from rounds 1-3, unaddressed: inline citations to Drepper's paper ('Drepper's paper explains in section 3.2', etc.) remain plain unlinked text, not tied to the numbered Sources list; the mobile hero (title, description, byline, date row, chip, collapsed TOC, prerequisite card) still consumes essentially the entire first 844px screen; and overflowing code blocks/tables at phone width still signal only via edge fade, no visible scroll affordance. This is round 4, the article's last round: the real, reproducible Lighthouse shortfall — which the pass gate treats as an unconditional requirement, not a critic's judgment call — is the dominant reason this cannot score at the 8.5 pass line, regardless of the genuine article-level polish achieved since round 3.
